title: Asking the way
topic: il y a / où est; prepositions of place; giving directions in the present; ordinals
why: After shopping and ordering, you now learn to find your way around a French town: asking where something is, understanding directions given in the present, and placing things with à côté de, en face de or au coin de. The lesson also looks closely at tu and vous, so you know whom to address how, and when to switch.

Excuse me, where is…?

You're in a French town and you're looking for the station, a pharmacy or a cash machine. There are three simple ways to ask, and all of them use words you already know. Always start with Bonjour or Excusez-moi: in France, a question fired at a stranger without a greeting sounds rude.

To ask…FrenchEnglish
the way to a placeExcusez-moi, pour aller à la gare ?Excuse me, how do I get to the station?
where a specific place isOù est la poste ?Where is the post office?
the same, a little more formalOù se trouve la mairie ?Where is the town hall?
if there is one nearbyIl y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?Is there a pharmacy near here?

Take Excusez-moi as a set phrase for now: it's an imperative, a form you'll study later. Se trouver (to be located) is a pronominal verb like se lever: la gare se trouve, les toilettes se trouvent.

Où est or il y a?

It works just like English. Où est + le / la asks for a specific place that you know exists: Où est la gare ? Il y a + un / une asks if there is any such place around: Il y a un distributeur près d'ici ? (Is there a cash machine near here?). And remember your contractions: pour aller au musée, à la gare, à l'hôtel, aux toilettes.

Understanding the answer

C'est tout près, à cinq minutes à pied.It's very close, five minutes' walk.
C'est un peu loin. Vous pouvez prendre le bus.It's a bit far. You can take the bus.
Désolé, je ne sais pas. Je ne suis pas d'ici.Sorry, I don't know. I'm not from around here.

Add Monsieur or Madame to your question: Pardon, Madame, où est la gare ? It sounds warm and polite, and nobody uses Mademoiselle anymore.

", "

Where things are: prepositions of place

To understand directions, you need the little words that place things in the street. Some take de, others don't: learn each one as a block.

FrenchEnglishExample
à côté denext toLa poste est à côté du musée.
en face deopposite, across fromLa pharmacie est en face de la gare.
près de / loin denear / far fromL'hôtel est près de la place.
au coin deat the corner ofLe café est au coin de la rue.
au bout deat the end ofLa mairie est au bout de la rue.
devant / derrièrein front of / behindLe parking est derrière la poste.
sur / souson / underLe plan est sur la table.
entre… et…between… and…La banque est entre le café et la boulangerie.
à gauche (de) / à droite (de)on the left (of) / on the right (of)La gare est à droite.
tout droitstraight aheadVous allez tout droit.

The trap: de + le = du

English says “next to the museum”, with no “of”. French needs de, and de contracts with le and les exactly as you've seen: à côté du musée (never à côté de le musée), en face des magasins, but en face de la gare and près de l'hôtel. On the other hand, devant, derrière, sur, sous and entre never take de: devant la mairie.

Il y a une boulangerie au coin de la rue, à côté du cinéma.There's a bakery at the corner of the street, next to the movie theater.
Le distributeur est entre la banque et la pharmacie.The cash machine is between the bank and the pharmacy.

À droite (on the right) and tout droit (straight ahead) sound alike and confuse everybody, French people included. If you have a doubt, point and ask: À droite ou tout droit ?

", "

Giving directions, and tu or vous?

To give directions, French people very often use the plain present with vous, where English uses an imperative (“Go straight on, turn left”). It sounds natural and polite, and you already know all the verbs. The real imperative will come later.

With vousWith tuEnglish
Vous allez tout droit.Tu vas tout droit.You go straight ahead.
Vous tournez à gauche.Tu tournes à gauche.You turn left.
Vous prenez la deuxième rue à droite.Tu prends la deuxième rue à droite.You take the second street on the right.
Vous traversez la place.Tu traverses la place.You cross the square.
Vous continuez jusqu'au feu.Tu continues jusqu'au feu.You keep going as far as the traffic light.

First, second, third

Ordinals are easy: number + -ième: deuxième, troisième, quatrième, dixième. Watch three details: cinq → cinquième (with a u), neuf → neuvième (f becomes v), and “first” is irregular and agrees: le premier carrefour, la première rue. Written short: 1er, 1re, 2e, 3e.

Tu or vous?

Use vous with strangers, in shops, with older people and at work until someone suggests otherwise. Use tu with friends, family, children, and often among young people. When you ask the way, it's always vous. When a relationship becomes friendlier, someone (usually the older person or the boss) proposes the switch: On se tutoie ? (Shall we say tu?). Saying tu too early can sound overfamiliar; saying vous too long can sound cold, but it's never rude.

If in doubt, say vous. The other person will tell you if they prefer tu.
